title: World
blurb: The planet and its people: seasons, time zones, languages and cities.

lessons.title: How the planet works
lessons.summary: Seasons, time zones, coordinates and the ocean's central heating.

cards.title: Why we have seasons
cards.text:
It isn't about distance: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, in the middle of our winter.

Seasons come from Earth's tilt of about 23.4°. In June the northern hemisphere leans toward the Sun, so sunlight hits it more directly and days are longer. In December it leans away.

cards.title: Try it: time zones
cards.text: Earth turns 360° a day, so each hour of time difference is about 15° of longitude. Countries round that off to suit their borders, and a few, like India, use half hours. Move Lisbon's clock (winter time) and watch the world follow.

cards.title: Latitude and longitude
cards.text:
Every place on Earth has two coordinates. Latitude says how far north or south of the equator you are, from 0° to 90°. Longitude says how far east or west of the Greenwich meridian in London, from 0° to 180°.

Viana do Castelo sits at about 41.7° N, 8.8° W.

cards.title: The ocean's central heating
cards.text:
Porto and New York sit at almost the same latitude, yet Porto's winters are far milder. Part of the reason is the Gulf Stream and its extension, which carry warm tropical water north-east across the Atlantic.

Westerly winds blowing off that warm ocean bring the heat ashore. Cold water returns south, completing a vast loop.

cards.title: Day and night

steps: Sun appears to rise in the east

cards.text: Earth spins once on its axis about every 24 hours, from west to east. That's why the Sun rises in the east and sets in the west, and why Japan sees sunrise hours before Portugal.

cards.title: The International Date Line
cards.text: Somewhere the calendar must change day. The date line runs roughly along 180° longitude through the Pacific; crossing it westward you jump a day ahead.

cards.title: Equinoxes and solstices
cards.text: Around 21 June, the northern hemisphere has its longest day (summer solstice); around 21 December its shortest. At the equinoxes in March and September, day and night are nearly equal everywhere.

cards.title: Daylight in Portugal
cards.text: In Lisbon, the longest day has about 14 h 50 min of daylight and the shortest about 9 h 30 min. Near the poles, summer brings the midnight sun.

cards.title: Earth's layers
cards.text: Beneath the thin crust lies the hot mantle, then a liquid outer core and a solid inner core about as hot as the Sun's surface.

cards.title: Plate tectonics
cards.text: Earth's crust is broken into plates that move a few centimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow. Where they meet, we get earthquakes, volcanoes and mountains.

quiz.q: What causes the seasons?
quiz.explain: The 23.4° tilt changes how directly sunlight hits each hemisphere through the year.

quiz.q: Two places are 45° of longitude apart. Roughly how many hours apart are their clocks?
Latitude measures…
quiz.explain: Latitude runs from 0° at the equator to 90° at the poles.

quiz.q: Why does the Sun rise in the east?
options: Earth spins from west to east
quiz.explain: Rotation makes the Sun appear to move.

quiz.q: About how fast do tectonic plates move?
quiz.explain: Roughly as fast as fingernails grow.

lessons.title: People and places
lessons.summary: Who lives where, what they speak, and why cities are where they are.

cards.title: If the world were 100 people
cards.text:
About 8 billion people live on Earth; the UN marked the milestone in November 2022. Shrink that to 100 people and roughly 59 live in Asia, 18 in Africa, 9 in Europe, 8 in Latin America, 5 in North America and 1 in Oceania.

India and China alone hold more than a third of humanity. Africa is the fastest-growing region.

cards.title: The most spoken languages
cards.text:
Count everyone who speaks a language, natives and learners together, and English comes first, with Mandarin Chinese second. Count only native speakers and Mandarin leads by a long way.

Portuguese has around 260 million speakers worldwide, most of them in Brazil, which makes it the most spoken language in the southern hemisphere.

cards.title: Why cities sit on rivers and coasts
cards.text:
Before railways and roads, water was the motorway. Rivers and sheltered harbours offered drinking water, fertile soil, fish and, above all, cheap transport for trade.

That's why so many great cities stand at a river mouth or a natural harbour: Lisbon on the Tagus, Porto on the Douro, London on the Thames, Shanghai at the mouth of the Yangtze.

cards.title: How many countries are there?
cards.text:
The usual answer is 195: the 193 members of the United Nations plus two observer states, the Vatican City and Palestine. Some places, like Taiwan and Kosovo, govern themselves but aren't UN members, so counts differ.

The largest is Russia, at about 17 million km². The smallest, Vatican City, is under half a square kilometre.

cards.title: Population growth
cards.text: World population took until about 1800 to reach 1 billion, then grew rapidly with better medicine and food: 2 billion in 1927, 4 billion in 1974, 8 billion in 2022.

cards.title: The most populous countries
cards.text: India overtook China as the most populous country in 2023, each with about 1.4 billion people. Then come the USA, Indonesia and Pakistan.

cards.title: Ageing populations
cards.text: Many rich countries, including Portugal, Italy and Japan, have low birth rates and long lives, so populations are ageing. Portugal has one of the oldest populations in Europe.

cards.title: Life expectancy
cards.text: Global life expectancy has more than doubled since 1900, from about 32 years to over 70. Portugal's is around 81 years.

cards.title: Migration
cards.text: About 280 million people live outside the country where they were born, around 3.5% of humanity. Portugal has been a country of emigration and, more recently, of immigration too.

cards.title: Portuguese around the world

items: Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau, São Tomé and Príncipe

cards.text: Portuguese is an official language in nine countries on four continents, from Brazil to Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde and Timor-Leste. Millions more Portuguese descendants live in France, the USA, Canada, Brazil and Switzerland.

quiz.q: Which region is home to most of the world's people?
quiz.explain: Roughly 59 out of every 100 people live in Asia.

quiz.q: Which language has the most native speakers?
quiz.explain: Mandarin leads on native speakers; English leads when learners are included.

quiz.q: Why did so many big cities grow on rivers and coasts?
options: Water, food and cheap transport for trade
Easier to defend from the air
quiz.explain: Water routes were the cheapest way to move goods and people for most of history.

quiz.q: Which country became the most populous in 2023?
World population reached 8 billion in…
quiz.explain: The UN marked it in November 2022.

lessons.title: Continents and oceans
lessons.summary: The big pieces of the world map.

cards.title: Seven continents
cards.text: The usual list is Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia/Oceania. Some countries count the Americas as one continent, or Europe and Asia as Eurasia.

cards.title: Five oceans
cards.text: The Pacific is the biggest, larger than all the land combined. Then come the Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic oceans.

cards.title: Mostly water
cards.text: About 71% of Earth's surface is ocean. Most fresh water is locked in ice; less than 1% of all water is fresh and easy to reach.

cards.title: The deepest point
cards.text: The Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, in the Pacific, is about 11 km deep, deeper than Everest is high.

cards.title: Pangaea
cards.text: About 300 million years ago, the continents were joined in a supercontinent called Pangaea. It broke apart slowly; South America and Africa still fit together like puzzle pieces.

cards.title: Where does Europe end?
cards.text: Europe and Asia share one landmass. By convention the boundary follows the Ural Mountains, the Ural River, the Caspian Sea and the Caucasus, which means Russia and Turkey span both.

cards.title: Islands
cards.text: Greenland is the world's largest island. Portugal's Atlantic islands, Madeira and the Azores, are volcanic; the Azores sit where three tectonic plates meet.

cards.title: Ocean currents
cards.text: Ocean currents act like conveyor belts, carrying heat around the planet. The Gulf Stream warms western Europe; the cold Canary Current runs down Portugal's coast, keeping summer seas cool.

cards.title: Seas and straits
cards.text: Narrow straits are vital shipping lanes: Gibraltar (Atlantic–Mediterranean), Suez Canal (Mediterranean–Red Sea), Hormuz (Persian Gulf), Malacca (Indian Ocean–Pacific), Panama Canal.

cards.title: Antarctica
cards.text: Antarctica is the coldest, driest and windiest continent, covered by ice up to 4.8 km thick. It holds about 70% of the world's fresh water. No country owns it; the 1959 Antarctic Treaty reserves it for science.

quiz.q: Which is the largest ocean?
What was Pangaea?
options: A supercontinent joining all the land
quiz.explain: It broke apart over millions of years.

quiz.q: What share of Earth's surface is ocean?
quiz.explain: Most of the planet is water.

lessons.title: Climates and biomes
lessons.summary: Why deserts, rainforests and tundra are where they are.

cards.title: Climate vs weather
cards.text: Weather is what happens today; climate is the average pattern over decades. "Climate is what you expect, weather is what you get."

cards.title: Latitude and sunlight
cards.text: Near the equator the Sun is high all year, so it's hot. Towards the poles, sunlight arrives at a low angle and is spread out, so it's cold.

cards.title: Climate zones
cards.text: The Köppen system classifies climates by temperature and rainfall. Most of Portugal has a Mediterranean climate (Csa/Csb): hot or warm dry summers and mild wet winters.

cards.title: Deserts
cards.text: Deserts get less than about 250 mm of rain a year. Many lie around 30° latitude, where dry air sinks. The Sahara is the largest hot desert; Antarctica is technically the largest desert of all.

cards.title: Rainforests
cards.text: Tropical rainforests grow near the equator with heat and rain all year. They cover about 6% of the land but hold over half of all species. The Amazon is the largest.

cards.title: Biomes
cards.text: A biome is a large region with similar climate, plants and animals: tropical rainforest, savanna, desert, Mediterranean scrub, temperate forest, taiga, tundra, grassland.

cards.title: Mountains change climate
cards.text: Temperature drops about 6.5 °C per 1,000 m of altitude. Serra da Estrela can be snowy while Lisbon is mild. Mountains also force air up, making one side wet and the other dry (rain shadow).

cards.title: Monsoons
cards.text: In South Asia, summer winds reverse and blow in from the warm ocean, bringing months of heavy rain. Over a billion people depend on the monsoon for farming.

cards.title: Portugal's contrasts
cards.text: The northwest (Minho) is one of Europe's rainiest regions; the interior Alentejo is hot and dry, often over 40 °C in summer. The Atlantic coast is mild; the interior has bigger temperature swings.

cards.title: Microclimates
cards.text: Cities are warmer than the countryside (urban heat islands); valleys collect cold air at night; coasts are milder. Vineyards and gardens exploit these small differences.

quiz.q: Most of Portugal has which climate?
quiz.explain: Hot dry summers, mild wet winters.

quiz.q: Roughly how much does temperature drop per 1,000 m of altitude?
What causes a rain shadow?
options: Mountains forcing air up so rain falls on one side

lessons.title: Rivers and mountains
lessons.summary: The world's great rivers and ranges.

cards.title: The longest rivers
cards.text: The Nile and the Amazon compete for the title of longest river, each around 6,400–7,000 km depending on how it's measured. The Amazon carries by far the most water.

cards.title: The Amazon's flow
cards.text: The Amazon discharges about 20% of all river water entering the oceans, more than the next seven largest rivers combined.

cards.title: Rivers and civilisation
cards.text: The first civilisations grew along rivers: the Nile, the Tigris and Euphrates, the Indus and the Yellow River, with water, fertile soil and transport.

cards.title: Portugal's rivers
cards.text: The Tejo (Tagus) is the longest river in Iberia, rising in Spain and reaching the sea at Lisbon. The Douro, Guadiana and Minho also start in Spain; the Mondego is the longest entirely Portuguese river.

cards.title: The highest mountains
cards.text: All fourteen peaks over 8,000 m are in the Himalaya and Karakoram in Asia. Everest, at 8,849 m, is the highest above sea level.

cards.title: Highest in Portugal
cards.text: Portugal's highest point is Mount Pico in the Azores, a volcano of 2,351 m. On the mainland, the highest is Torre in the Serra da Estrela, at 1,993 m.

cards.title: How mountains form
cards.text: Most great ranges form where tectonic plates collide and crumple: the Himalaya (India hitting Asia), the Alps (Africa pushing into Europe). Others are volcanic, like the Andes' peaks.

cards.title: Glaciers
cards.text: Glaciers are rivers of ice that carve U-shaped valleys and fjords. They store fresh water but are shrinking almost everywhere as the climate warms.

cards.title: Lakes
cards.text: The Caspian Sea is the largest lake by area; Lake Baikal in Siberia is the deepest and oldest, holding about a fifth of the world's unfrozen surface fresh water.

cards.title: Waterfalls
cards.text: Angel Falls in Venezuela is the tallest waterfall (979 m). Victoria Falls and Iguaçu are among the widest and most spectacular.

quiz.q: Which river carries the most water?
quiz.explain: About a fifth of world river discharge.

quiz.q: What is Portugal's highest point?
How did the Himalaya form?
options: The Indian plate colliding with Asia

lessons.title: Europe
lessons.summary: A small continent with many countries and languages.

cards.title: Many countries in little space
cards.text: Europe has about 44–50 countries depending on how you count, with around 745 million people, on just 7% of the world's land.

cards.title: The European Union
cards.text: The EU has 27 member states that share a single market, free movement of people and many common laws. 21 of them use the euro; Bulgaria was the latest to join, in 2026.

cards.title: Schengen
cards.text: In the Schengen area, people cross borders without passport checks. It includes most EU countries plus Norway, Iceland, Switzerland and Liechtenstein.

cards.title: Languages
cards.text: The EU has 24 official languages. Most European languages belong to the Indo-European family: Romance (Portuguese, Spanish, French, Italian), Germanic (English, German, Dutch) and Slavic (Polish, Czech).

cards.title: Basque: a mystery
cards.text: Basque (Euskara), spoken in northern Spain and southwestern France, is unrelated to any other known language, probably older than the Indo-European languages around it.

cards.title: Big economies
cards.text: Germany is Europe's largest economy, followed by the UK and France. Portugal's economy is mid-sized, with tourism, services, exports and manufacturing.

cards.title: Microstates
cards.text: Europe has tiny countries: Vatican City (0.44 km²), Monaco, San Marino, Liechtenstein and Andorra, which borders Spain and France high in the Pyrenees.

cards.title: Rivers and mountains of Europe
cards.text: The Volga is Europe's longest river; the Danube flows through ten countries. The Alps are the highest range, with Mont Blanc at 4,806 m.

cards.title: Iberia

items.l: Strait of Gibraltar at its narrowest

cards.text: Portugal and Spain share the Iberian Peninsula, with Andorra and Gibraltar (British). The peninsula is separated from Africa by the 14 km Strait of Gibraltar.

cards.title: The north–south and east–west divides
cards.text: Europe's regions differ in climate, economy and history: Nordic welfare states, the industrial centre, the Mediterranean south, and former communist countries in the east.

quiz.q: How many countries are in the EU?
Basque is related to…
Which is Europe's longest river?

lessons.title: Portugal's geography
lessons.summary: Districts, regions, rivers and islands.

cards.title: Shape and size
cards.text: Mainland Portugal is a rectangle about 560 km long and 220 km wide. With the Azores and Madeira, the country covers about 92,000 km² and has around 10.6 million people.

cards.title: Mainland and islands
cards.text: Portugal includes two autonomous regions in the Atlantic: the Azores (nine islands) and Madeira (Madeira, Porto Santo and uninhabited islets).

cards.title: North and south
cards.text: The north is greener, more mountainous and densely populated near the coast; the south is flatter and drier, with the Alentejo's plains and the Algarve's beaches. The Tejo roughly divides them.

cards.title: Coast and interior
cards.text: Most people live near the coast between Viana do Castelo and Setúbal. The interior has been losing population for decades, a challenge for services and fire prevention.

cards.title: Regions of the mainland
cards.text: Common regions (NUTS II): Norte, Centro, Área Metropolitana de Lisboa, Alentejo and Algarve. Older provinces like Minho, Trás-os-Montes and Beira are still used in everyday speech.

cards.title: The Minho

items: Ponte de Lima, Portugal's oldest town charter (1125)

cards.text: The Minho, in the far northwest, is green and rainy, known for vinho verde, granite villages, the Lima and Minho rivers, and towns like Viana do Castelo, Ponte de Lima and Braga.

cards.title: Peneda-Gerês
cards.text: Portugal's only national park, created in 1971, protects granite mountains, oak forests, wild Garrano horses, wolves and traditional villages along the Spanish border.

cards.title: Rivers and dams
cards.text: Portugal's big rivers have many dams for hydropower and water storage. The Alqueva reservoir on the Guadiana, completed in 2002, is one of Western Europe's largest artificial lakes.

cards.title: The Azores
cards.text: The Azores lie about 1,400 km west of Lisbon on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. They're volcanic, green and famous for crater lakes, hot springs, whales and tea plantations.

cards.title: Madeira
cards.text: Madeira, about 1,000 km southwest of Lisbon, is a steep volcanic island with laurel forests (UNESCO), levadas (irrigation channels with walking paths) and its famous fortified wine.

quiz.q: What is Portugal's only national park?
Which large reservoir is on the Guadiana?
How many islands make up the Azores?

lessons.title: Africa
lessons.summary: A huge, young and diverse continent.

cards.title: Bigger than it looks
cards.text: Common world maps shrink Africa. It's bigger than the USA, China, India and most of Europe combined, at about 30 million km².

cards.title: 54 countries
cards.text: Africa has 54 UN member states. Nigeria is the most populous (over 220 million), Algeria the largest by area.

cards.title: The youngest continent
cards.text: Africa's median age is about 19, compared with about 44 in Europe. By 2050, roughly a quarter of the world's people may live in Africa.

cards.title: Languages
cards.text: Over 2,000 languages are spoken in Africa. Arabic, Swahili, Hausa, Amharic and Yoruba each have tens of millions of speakers. Portuguese is official in five countries.

cards.title: Portuguese-speaking Africa
cards.text: Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau and São Tomé and Príncipe make up the PALOP. Luanda and Maputo are big, fast-growing cities.

cards.title: Natural wonders
cards.text: The Sahara desert, the Nile, Mount Kilimanjaro, Victoria Falls, the Serengeti's migrations and the Okavango Delta are among the world's great natural sights.

cards.title: Resources
cards.text: Africa holds large shares of the world's cobalt, platinum, diamonds, cocoa and many other resources. Turning them into broad prosperity remains a challenge.

cards.title: Mobile money

steps: Pay and send money by SMS

cards.text: Africa leapt ahead with mobile money: Kenya's M-Pesa, launched in 2007, lets millions pay, save and send money by phone without a bank account.

cards.title: The cradle of humankind
cards.text: Africa is where humans evolved. Fossils such as "Lucy" (3.2 million years old, Ethiopia) and the oldest Homo sapiens remains (about 300,000 years, Morocco) were found there.

cards.title: Growth and challenges
cards.text: Many African economies are among the world's fastest growing, with booming tech hubs in Lagos, Nairobi and Kigali. Challenges include poverty, conflict in some regions and climate risks.

quiz.q: Which is Africa's most populous country?
What is Africa's median age, approximately?
In how many African countries is Portuguese official?
quiz.explain: Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau, São Tomé and Príncipe.

lessons.title: Asia
lessons.summary: The largest continent, home to most of humanity.

cards.title: Scale
cards.text: Asia covers about 30% of Earth's land and holds nearly 60% of its people. It stretches from Turkey to Japan and from Siberia to Indonesia.

cards.title: Regions

items: West and Central: Middle East, Kazakhstan

cards.text: Asia is usually split into East, South, Southeast, Central and West Asia (the Middle East), each with very different histories, religions and climates.

cards.title: China
cards.text: China has about 1.4 billion people, the world's second-largest economy and a history of continuous civilisation over 3,500 years. Mandarin Chinese has the most native speakers of any language.

cards.title: India
cards.text: India is the world's most populous country and largest democracy, with 22 scheduled languages and a booming technology sector. Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism were born on the subcontinent.

cards.title: Japan
cards.text: Japan blends ancient traditions with advanced technology. Its population is shrinking and ageing fast; nearly 30% of people are over 65.

cards.title: Portuguese traces in Asia
cards.text: Portuguese traders left words and places across Asia: "pão" became "pan" in Japanese, tempura has Portuguese roots, Macau was Portuguese until 1999, and Kristang creole is still spoken in Malacca.

cards.title: The Middle East

items: About half of world oil reserves

cards.text: West Asia holds about half of the world's proven oil reserves and the holy sites of Judaism, Christianity and Islam in Jerusalem, Mecca and Medina.

cards.title: Economic tigers
cards.text: South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Hong Kong grew from poverty to wealth in a few decades through exports, education and technology. Today Taiwan makes most of the world's advanced chips.

cards.title: Rivers and mountains
cards.text: Asia has the Himalaya, the Gobi desert, the Siberian taiga and great rivers like the Yangtze, Ganges, Mekong and Indus, which feed hundreds of millions of people.

cards.title: Megacities
cards.text: Many of the world's largest cities are in Asia: Tokyo, Delhi, Shanghai, Dhaka, Mumbai, Beijing and others with populations over 20 million in their urban areas.

quiz.q: Who were the first Europeans to reach Japan?
Until when was Macau administered by Portugal?
Roughly what share of humanity lives in Asia?

lessons.title: The Americas
lessons.summary: Two continents from the Arctic to Cape Horn.

cards.title: North, Central, South
cards.text: The Americas stretch about 14,000 km from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego. North America includes Canada, the USA and Mexico; Central America links to South America at Panama.

cards.title: First peoples
cards.text: People reached the Americas from Asia at least 15,000 years ago. Great civilisations followed: the Maya, the Aztecs with their capital Tenochtitlan, and the Inca empire in the Andes.

cards.title: European conquest
cards.text: After 1492, Spanish and Portuguese colonisation, followed by English, French and Dutch, transformed the Americas. Disease, war and forced labour killed a huge share of the native population.

cards.title: Brazil
cards.text: Brazil is the largest country in South America, with about 215 million people, the Amazon rainforest and the largest Portuguese-speaking population in the world.

cards.title: The USA
cards.text: The USA is the world's largest economy, with 50 states and about 340 million people. Its culture, technology and companies have global influence.

cards.title: Canada
cards.text: Canada is the world's second-largest country by area but has only about 40 million people, mostly living near the US border. English and French are official languages.

cards.title: Spanish and Portuguese America
cards.text: Spanish is spoken from Mexico to Argentina; Portuguese in Brazil. Spanish speakers in the Americas outnumber those in Spain by about ten to one.

cards.title: The Andes and the Amazon
cards.text: The Andes are the world's longest mountain range on land, about 7,000 km. To their east, the Amazon basin holds the largest rainforest on Earth.

cards.title: The Panama Canal

items.l: saved on a New York–San Francisco voyage

cards.text: Opened in 1914, the canal lets ships cross between the Atlantic and Pacific without going around South America, saving about 13,000 km.

cards.title: Food from the Americas
cards.text: The Americas gave the world maize, potatoes, tomatoes, chillies, cocoa, vanilla, peanuts and turkeys. Imagine Portuguese food without potatoes and tomatoes!

quiz.q: Who reached Brazil in 1500?
quiz.explain: Cabral, on his way to India.

quiz.q: Which country is second largest by area?
Which foods came from the Americas?

lessons.title: Oceania and the poles
lessons.summary: Islands, Australia and the frozen ends of the Earth.

cards.title: Oceania
cards.text: Oceania includes Australia, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea and thousands of Pacific islands grouped as Melanesia, Micronesia and Polynesia.

cards.title: Australia

items.l: live within 50 km of the coast

cards.text: Australia is both a country and a continent, mostly dry outback with most people living on the coast. It's home to unique animals like kangaroos, koalas and platypuses.

cards.title: Aboriginal Australians
cards.text: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived in Australia for at least 50,000 years, one of the oldest continuous cultures on Earth.

cards.title: The Great Barrier Reef
cards.text: Off northeast Australia, the Great Barrier Reef stretches over 2,300 km, the largest structure built by living things. Warming seas cause coral bleaching.

cards.title: New Zealand

events.l: first country to give women the vote

cards.text: New Zealand's two main islands have volcanoes, glaciers and fjords. The Māori arrived around 1300 CE, among the last large lands settled by humans.

cards.title: Polynesian navigators
cards.text: Polynesians crossed thousands of kilometres of open Pacific in double canoes, navigating by stars, swells and birds, reaching Hawaii, Easter Island and New Zealand.

cards.title: The Arctic
cards.text: The Arctic is an ocean surrounded by land, mostly covered by floating sea ice. It's warming about three to four times faster than the global average, shrinking summer ice.

cards.title: Polar day and night
cards.text: Above the Arctic Circle, the Sun never sets around the summer solstice and never rises around the winter solstice. At the poles themselves, there are six months of day and six of night.

cards.title: Life in the cold
cards.text: Inuit, Sámi and other Arctic peoples have adapted to extreme cold for thousands of years. Animals use fat, fur and migration; Antarctic fish have antifreeze proteins in their blood.

cards.title: Pacific islands and the sea
cards.text: Low-lying Pacific nations like Tuvalu and Kiribati are only a few metres above sea level and are among the most threatened by rising seas.

quiz.q: How long have Aboriginal Australians lived in Australia?
quiz.explain: One of the oldest continuous cultures.

quiz.q: Which was the first country to give women the vote, in 1893?
The Arctic is mainly…
options: An ocean covered by sea ice

lessons.title: How the world earns a living
lessons.summary: GDP, trade and why some countries are richer.

cards.title: GDP
cards.text: Gross domestic product is the total value of goods and services produced in a country in a year. It measures the size of an economy, not how well off people are.

cards.title: The biggest economies
cards.text: The USA is the largest economy, followed by China, Germany, Japan and India. Measured by purchasing power, China is the largest.

cards.title: GDP per person
cards.text: Dividing GDP by population gives a better sense of average income. Luxembourg, Ireland and Switzerland rank high; Portugal is mid-table in the EU.

cards.title: Sectors
cards.text: Economies have three broad sectors: primary (farming, mining), secondary (industry) and tertiary (services). Rich countries are mostly services; Portugal's tourism is a major service export.

cards.title: Trade
cards.text: Countries specialise in what they do relatively well and trade. Portugal exports cars, machinery, fuels, clothing, cork, wine and tourism, mainly to Spain, France and Germany.

cards.title: Inflation
cards.text: Inflation is a general rise in prices. The European Central Bank aims for about 2% a year. In 2022 inflation spiked across Europe with energy prices.

cards.title: Interest rates
cards.text: Central banks raise interest rates to cool inflation and lower them to encourage borrowing and growth. Mortgage payments in Portugal, mostly variable-rate, follow the Euribor.

cards.title: Supply and demand
cards.text: Prices rise when demand outstrips supply, and fall when supply exceeds demand. Commodity markets, like wheat or soybeans, react quickly to harvests, weather and wars.

cards.title: Why some countries are rich
cards.text: Economists point to institutions (rule of law, low corruption), education, infrastructure, technology, trade openness and stability. Natural resources alone don't guarantee wealth.

cards.title: Inequality
cards.text: The Gini index measures inequality from 0 (everyone equal) to 1 (one person has everything). Nordic countries have low inequality; South Africa and Brazil high. Portugal is around the EU average.

quiz.q: What does GDP measure?
options: The total value of goods and services produced

quiz.q: What does the ECB usually do to fight high inflation?
What share of Portugal's economy is services?

lessons.title: Feeding the world
lessons.summary: Crops, commodities and how food travels.

cards.title: The big crops
cards.text: Just a few crops supply most of humanity's calories: maize, rice, wheat and soybeans, plus sugar cane and palm oil.

cards.title: Where they grow
cards.text: The USA, China and Brazil lead maize; China and India rice; China, India and Russia wheat; Brazil and the USA soybeans. Weather in a few regions can move world prices.

cards.title: Most soy feeds animals
cards.text: About three-quarters of soybeans are crushed into meal for animal feed (chickens, pigs, fish), with the oil used for cooking and biodiesel.

cards.title: Commodity trading
cards.text: Global traders buy grain and oilseeds from farmers, store them, ship them and sell them to millers, crushers and food companies worldwide, managing price, quality and logistics risks.

cards.title: Futures and hedging

items: exposed if prices fall or rise

cards.text: Futures contracts fix a price today for delivery later. Farmers and traders use them to hedge price risk. The Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) sets benchmark prices for corn, soybeans and wheat.

cards.title: Shipping routes
cards.text: Grain moves on bulk carriers through key chokepoints: the Panama Canal, the Black Sea, the Suez Canal and the Strait of Malacca. Disruptions raise freight costs and prices.

cards.title: Coffee and cocoa
cards.text: Coffee grows mostly in Brazil, Vietnam and Colombia; cocoa mainly in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana. Both are traded worldwide and sensitive to weather and plant disease.

cards.title: Food waste

items.l: of food lost or wasted (FAO estimate)

cards.text: Roughly a third of food produced is lost or wasted, from field to fridge. Reducing waste is one of the easiest ways to feed more people with less land and emissions.

cards.title: Fertilisers
cards.text: Modern yields depend on fertilisers. Nitrogen fertiliser made with the Haber–Bosch process feeds roughly half the world's population, but uses natural gas and causes pollution if overused.

cards.title: Portugal's food
cards.text: Portugal imports most of its cereals but exports wine, olive oil, tomatoes, fruit and cork. Olive groves in the Alentejo have expanded hugely thanks to Alqueva irrigation.

quiz.q: Most soybean meal is used for…
What does a futures contract do?
options: Fixes a price today for later delivery

quiz.q: Roughly how much food is lost or wasted?

lessons.title: Energy around the world
lessons.summary: How the world powers itself, and how that's changing.

cards.title: Primary energy mix
cards.text: Fossil fuels (oil, coal, gas) still supply about 80% of the world's primary energy. Renewables and nuclear make up the rest, growing quickly in electricity.

cards.title: Electricity vs energy
cards.text: Electricity is only about 20% of final energy use. Transport, heating and industry still burn fuels directly, which is why electrifying them matters.

cards.title: Solar's rise

events.l: cheapest new power in many places

cards.text: Solar power has become the cheapest electricity in history in many places. Global solar capacity grew more than tenfold in a decade.

cards.title: Oil
cards.text: Oil fuels most transport. The biggest producers are the USA, Saudi Arabia and Russia. OPEC+ coordinates production to influence prices.

cards.title: Gas and Europe
cards.text: Europe imported much of its gas from Russia until 2022. After the invasion of Ukraine, it switched to LNG from the USA, Qatar and others. Portugal's Sines terminal receives LNG.

cards.title: Coal

items.l: of world coal burned in China

cards.text: Coal is the most carbon-intensive fuel. China burns over half the world's coal. Portugal closed its last coal power plants in 2021.

cards.title: Energy per person

viz.unit: kWh per person per year (primary, approx.)

cards.text: Energy use per person varies hugely: an average American uses several times more than an average Portuguese and dozens of times more than someone in many African countries.

cards.title: Hydrogen
cards.text: Green hydrogen, made by splitting water with renewable electricity, could fuel steelmaking, fertiliser and shipping. Portugal is planning projects, notably around Sines.

cards.title: Energy security
cards.text: Countries want energy that's affordable, reliable and not dependent on a single supplier. Renewables, storage, interconnections and efficiency improve security.

cards.title: Energy transition
cards.text: The world is shifting from fossil fuels to clean electricity, but the transition requires huge investment in grids, storage, minerals and new industries.

quiz.q: About how much of world primary energy still comes from fossil fuels?
quiz.explain: Oil, coal and gas still dominate.

quiz.q: When did Portugal stop burning coal for power?
What is green hydrogen made with?

lessons.title: Water
lessons.summary: A precious and unevenly shared resource.

cards.title: Fresh water is scarce
cards.text: Only about 2.5% of Earth's water is fresh, and most of that is frozen in ice caps and glaciers or deep underground. Rivers and lakes hold a tiny fraction.

cards.title: The water cycle
cards.text: The Sun evaporates water from oceans and land; it condenses into clouds, falls as rain or snow, and flows back via rivers and groundwater. The cycle never stops.

cards.title: Farming uses most
cards.text: Agriculture accounts for about 70% of fresh water withdrawals worldwide. Drip irrigation, used widely in the Alentejo, can cut water use dramatically.

cards.title: Virtual water
cards.text: Producing goods uses water. A cup of coffee takes about 140 litres along the supply chain; a kilo of beef around 15,000 litres.

cards.title: Access to safe water
cards.text: About 2 billion people still lack safely managed drinking water, and many more lack safe sanitation, mostly in rural areas of Africa and Asia.

cards.title: Drought in Iberia
cards.text: Southern Portugal and Spain face more frequent droughts. Reservoirs like Alqueva, desalination plans in the Algarve and water reuse help, along with careful farming.

cards.title: Desalination
cards.text: Desalination removes salt from seawater, mostly by reverse osmosis. It's reliable but energy-intensive. Countries like Israel and Saudi Arabia rely heavily on it.

cards.title: Shared rivers
cards.text: Many rivers cross borders. Portugal and Spain manage their shared rivers under the 1998 Albufeira Convention, which sets minimum flows Spain must let through.

cards.title: Groundwater
cards.text: Aquifers store water underground. Pumping faster than rain refills them lowers water tables and can let seawater in near coasts.

cards.title: Saving water at home
cards.text: Fixing leaks, efficient taps and showers, full loads in the dishwasher and washing machine, and collecting rainwater for the garden all cut use.

quiz.q: Which sector uses most fresh water?
Which agreement manages rivers shared by Portugal and Spain?
How is most seawater desalinated?
quiz.explain: High pressure pushes water through membranes.

lessons.title: International organisations
lessons.summary: How countries cooperate.

cards.title: The United Nations
cards.text: Founded in 1945, the UN has 193 member states. The General Assembly gives each one vote; the Security Council handles peace and security.

cards.title: The Security Council
cards.text: It has 15 members: five permanent ones with veto power (USA, UK, France, Russia, China) and ten elected for two years. Portugal last served in 2011–12.

cards.title: António Guterres
cards.text: Former Portuguese prime minister António Guterres became UN Secretary-General in 2017, after leading the UN Refugee Agency. His second term runs to the end of 2026.

cards.title: UN agencies
cards.text: Specialised agencies work on health (WHO), food (FAO, WFP), children (UNICEF), refugees (UNHCR), culture (UNESCO) and more.

cards.title: The EU institutions
cards.text: The European Commission proposes laws, the Parliament (elected) and Council (national governments) adopt them, and the Court of Justice interprets them.

cards.title: NATO
cards.text: NATO is a military alliance founded in 1949. An attack on one member is treated as an attack on all (Article 5). It has 32 members after Finland and Sweden joined in 2023–24.

cards.title: Economic organisations
cards.text: The IMF lends to countries in crisis (including Portugal in 2011), the World Bank funds development, the WTO sets trade rules and the OECD compares policies among richer countries.

cards.title: The CPLP

items: Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau, São Tomé, Timor-Leste, Equatorial Guinea

cards.text: The Community of Portuguese Language Countries, founded in 1996, links nine countries where Portuguese is official, promoting the language and cooperation.

cards.title: International courts
cards.text: The International Court of Justice settles disputes between states; the International Criminal Court prosecutes individuals for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity. Both sit in The Hague.

cards.title: Limits of cooperation
cards.text: International organisations depend on members' willingness. Vetoes, unpaid budgets and rivalries limit what they can do, but they remain the main forums for global problems.

quiz.q: How many permanent members does the UN Security Council have?
Which Portuguese politician became UN Secretary-General in 2017?
quiz.explain: He'd led the UN Refugee Agency.

quiz.q: What does NATO's Article 5 say?
options: An attack on one is an attack on all

lessons.title: World religions and cultures
lessons.summary: Beliefs, festivals and customs, in brief.

cards.title: Major religions
cards.text: Christianity and Islam are the largest religions, followed by Hinduism and Buddhism. About 15% of people are unaffiliated with any religion.

cards.title: Abrahamic religions
cards.text: Judaism, Christianity and Islam share roots in the figure of Abraham and belief in one God. Jerusalem is sacred to all three.

cards.title: Religions of India and East Asia
cards.text: Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism began in South Asia. Confucianism, Taoism and Shinto shaped China and Japan, often blended with Buddhism.

cards.title: Religion in Portugal
cards.text: Most Portuguese identify as Catholic, though regular practice has declined. Fátima, where Marian apparitions were reported in 1917, is one of the world's major pilgrimage sites.

cards.title: Calendars
cards.text: Most of the world uses the Gregorian calendar (1582). The Islamic calendar is lunar, so Ramadan moves about 11 days earlier each year. Chinese New Year follows a lunisolar calendar.

cards.title: Festivals of light
cards.text: Many cultures celebrate light in the dark season: Diwali (Hindu), Hanukkah (Jewish), Christmas (Christian) and Lunar New Year lanterns.

cards.title: Greetings around the world
cards.text: Customs differ: handshakes, bows in Japan, cheek kisses in Portugal and France (two kisses in Portugal), the wai in Thailand, namaste in India.

cards.title: Time and punctuality
cards.text: Attitudes to time vary: Swiss and German meetings start exactly on time; in many Mediterranean and Latin American cultures, schedules are more flexible. Knowing the norms avoids misunderstandings.

cards.title: High and low context
cards.text: In low-context cultures (Germany, Netherlands, USA), people say things explicitly. In high-context cultures (Japan, China, Arab countries), much is implied by relationship and situation.

cards.title: UNESCO heritage
cards.text: UNESCO lists over 1,200 World Heritage sites. Portugal has 17, including the Jerónimos Monastery, Sintra, the historic centres of Porto, Évora and Guimarães, and the Douro wine region.

quiz.q: How many cheek kisses are usual in Portugal?
quiz.explain: Two, starting with the right cheek.

quiz.q: Why does Ramadan move earlier each year?
options: The Islamic calendar is lunar, about 11 days shorter

quiz.q: Which three religions consider Jerusalem sacred?

lessons.title: Cities
lessons.summary: Urbanisation, megacities and liveable places.

cards.title: An urban planet
cards.text: Since about 2007, more people live in cities than in the countryside. By 2050 about two-thirds of humanity is expected to be urban.

cards.title: Megacities
cards.text: Cities with over 10 million people are megacities. There are over 30 today, most in Asia: Tokyo, Delhi, Shanghai, São Paulo, Mexico City, Cairo, Mumbai.

cards.title: Why cities grow
cards.text: Cities offer jobs, education, healthcare and opportunity. Clustering people and firms boosts productivity and innovation.

cards.title: Lisbon and Porto
cards.text: Lisbon's metropolitan area has about 2.9 million people, Porto's about 1.8 million. Together they hold nearly half of Portugal's population.

cards.title: Informal settlements

items.l: people in slums or informal settlements (UN estimate)

cards.text: About a billion people live in slums or informal settlements without secure housing, clean water or sanitation, mostly in fast-growing cities of Africa and Asia.

cards.title: Transport
cards.text: Good public transport, cycling and walking make cities more liveable. Lisbon's trams and metro, Porto's metro (opened 2002) and new bus rapid transit lines aim to reduce car dependence.

cards.title: The 15-minute city
cards.text: The idea: everyday needs like shops, schools, health and parks should be reachable within 15 minutes on foot or by bike. Paris has promoted it since 2020.

cards.title: Heat in cities
cards.text: Concrete and asphalt absorb heat, making cities several degrees warmer than surrounding countryside. Trees, parks, light-coloured roofs and water features cool them.

cards.title: Housing pressure
cards.text: Many popular cities, including Lisbon and Porto, face rising rents and house prices driven by demand, tourism and limited supply. Governments try new construction, rent rules and limits on short-term rentals.

cards.title: Smart cities
cards.text: Sensors and data help cities manage traffic lights, parking, waste collection, water leaks and air quality more efficiently.

lessons.title: Climate change
lessons.summary: What's happening, why, and what can be done.

cards.title: The greenhouse effect
cards.text: Greenhouse gases like CO₂ and methane let sunlight in but trap some of the heat Earth radiates. Without them Earth would be about −18 °C on average; with more of them, it warms.

cards.title: CO₂ is rising
cards.text: CO₂ in the air was about 280 parts per million before industry. It passed 420 ppm in 2023, the highest in at least 800,000 years.

cards.title: How much warmer?
cards.text: The world is about 1.2–1.3 °C warmer than pre-industrial times on average. 2024 was the warmest year on record, around 1.5 °C above the pre-industrial average.

cards.title: Where emissions come from
cards.text: Most emissions come from burning fossil fuels for electricity and heat, transport, industry and buildings. Agriculture and land use (deforestation, livestock) add a large share.

cards.title: Impacts
cards.text: Warming brings more heatwaves, droughts, wildfires and heavy rain; rising seas; shrinking glaciers and sea ice; and stress on crops and ecosystems.

cards.title: Portugal's risks

items: Droughts in the Alentejo and Algarve

cards.text: Portugal is among Europe's most exposed countries: hotter summers, longer droughts in the south, more severe wildfires, and coastal erosion along the Atlantic.

cards.title: The Paris Agreement
cards.text: Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, almost every country agreed to limit warming to well below 2 °C, aiming for 1.5 °C, with national plans updated every five years.

cards.title: Net zero
cards.text: Net zero means cutting emissions as close to zero as possible and balancing the rest with removals (forests, carbon capture). Portugal aims for climate neutrality by 2045.

cards.title: Solutions
cards.text: The biggest levers: clean electricity, electrified transport and heating, efficient buildings and industry, protecting forests, less food waste and changes in diet.

cards.title: Adaptation
cards.text: Even with cuts, some change is locked in. Adaptation means preparing: heat plans, fire-resistant landscapes, water storage, flood defences and resilient crops.

lessons.title: Natural hazards
lessons.summary: Earthquakes, volcanoes, storms and how to prepare.

cards.title: Earthquakes
cards.text: Earthquakes happen when stress along a fault is suddenly released. Most occur at plate boundaries. Portugal sits near the boundary between the Eurasian and African plates.

cards.title: Magnitude
cards.text: Magnitude scales are logarithmic: each whole step releases about 32 times more energy. A magnitude 8 releases about 1,000 times more energy than a magnitude 6.

cards.title: What to do in an earthquake

steps: After shaking: coast? Go to high ground

cards.text: Drop, cover and hold on: get under a sturdy table, protect your head and hold on until shaking stops. Stay away from windows. Near the coast, move to high ground if shaking is strong or long.

cards.title: Tsunamis
cards.text: Undersea earthquakes can lift the sea floor and launch tsunamis that cross oceans at jet speed. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed around 230,000 people.

cards.title: Volcanoes
cards.text: Volcanoes form where magma reaches the surface, at plate boundaries or hotspots. The Azores have active volcanoes; Capelinhos on Faial erupted in 1957–58, adding new land.

cards.title: Hurricanes and typhoons
cards.text: Tropical cyclones form over warm oceans (above about 26.5 °C). They're called hurricanes in the Atlantic, typhoons in the northwest Pacific and cyclones in the Indian Ocean.

cards.title: Wildfires
cards.text: Hot, dry, windy weather plus fuel (dense undergrowth, eucalyptus and pine plantations) makes fires spread fast. In 2017, wildfires in Portugal killed over 100 people.

cards.title: Floods
cards.text: Floods come from heavy rain, rivers overflowing, storm surges and flash floods in steep valleys. Building on flood plains increases the damage.

cards.title: Heatwaves

items: Never leave anyone in a parked car

cards.text: Heatwaves are the deadliest weather hazard in Europe, especially for older people. Drink water, stay cool, check on vulnerable neighbours and avoid the midday sun.

cards.title: Preparedness
cards.text: Know your local risks, have an emergency kit (water, torch, radio, medicines, documents), agree a family meeting point and follow official alerts from Proteção Civil.
